title: Nielsen Sports SA puts 150 million sports fan data points behind AI platform
article_text:
- Nielsen Sports SA has launched SIYA (Sponsorship Intelligence Yielding Answers), an AI-powered platform that gives users faster access to sports fan insights through natural-language questions.

- SIYA provides access to more than 150 million sports fan data points, helping brands, broadcasters, rights holders and agencies explore South African sports audience behaviour.

- Unlike generative AI tools that may produce inaccurate information, SIYA retrieves statistics from Nielsen Sports SA’s verified research using governed queries and established rules for respondent eligibility and data weighting.

- SIYA enables sports marketers and media organisations to investigate fan behaviour, viewing platforms, beverage preferences, betting habits and sponsor associations, supporting sponsorship evaluation and media planning.

- Nielsen Sports SA plans to expand SIYA with sports consumption and viewership data, sponsorship news, proprietary research and travel and tourism insights, creating a broader picture of sports fans’ behaviour and commercial value.

Nielsen Sports SA has launched SIYA (Sponsorship Intelligence Yielding Answers), an AI-powered platform designed to give brands, broadcasters, rights holders and agencies faster access to sports fan insights without having to commission research or wait for an analyst to interpret the data.

The platform gives users access to more than 150 million sports fan data points through natural-language prompts, allowing them to ask questions about South African sports audiences and receive answers within minutes.

According to Tumelo Selikane, managing director of Nielsen Sports SA, the platform addresses a gap between the amount of sports research available and the time and expertise required to access it.

“The insight already existed, but it was locked behind time and specialists,” he says. “A brand, broadcaster or rights holder with a question about South African sports fans had to commission a study or wait for an analyst to pull it, which could take days.”

SIYA is designed to make that process self-service, allowing users to interrogate Nielsen Sports SA’s existing fan research when they need an answer.

With growing concerns about the reliability of AI-generated information, Nielsen says SIYA does not generate statistics. Instead, it retrieves data from its verified research using governed queries.

“SIYA does not generate numbers; it retrieves them,” says Selikane. “Every figure comes from a governed query against our actual Nielsen Sports SA survey data.”

The platform applies the same rules an analyst would, including ensuring that only respondents who were genuinely asked a particular question are counted and identifying whether figures are weighted or unweighted.

“The AI interprets the question and presents the answer in plain language, but it cannot invent data,” Selikane says. “When a question falls outside what the underlying research supports, SIYA states that rather than guessing.”

The platform is also being developed for multilingual use. Users can ask questions in their own words, with Nielsen building support across South Africa’s official languages in phases.

Selikane says the challenge is not simply translating a question or answer, but ensuring that statistical meaning and caveats remain intact.

“The genuinely hard part is not translating the words; it is making sure a statistic and its caveats survive translation intact,” he says.

Nielsen expects the faster turnaround to change how organisations use research in sponsorship, audience and media decisions.

“When an answer takes days, you only ask the big, pre-planned questions,” says Selikane. “When it takes a minute, you can test an idea in the room, follow a hunch, and check three options before you commit budget.”

Early users have included sponsorship agencies, broadcasters, a global sports league, a major technology platform and brands outside traditional sports marketing, including education and FMCG.

The questions have also extended beyond the size of a particular fan base.

Users have asked about what fans drink, whether they bet, which platforms they watch on and which sponsors they already associate with teams, looking for potential commercial connections.

Some users have gone further, asking SIYA to help shape media strategies rather than simply provide audience insights.

Nielsen developed SIYA internally over the past year, with Selikane saying control over accuracy was a key reason for taking that approach.

“An off-the-shelf assistant is very good at sounding confident, including when it is wrong, which is the opposite of what a research business can put its name to,” he says.

Building the platform internally allows Nielsen to connect the model directly to its verified data, apply its own rules around bases and weighting, and retain control over client and respondent data.

SIYA is not intended to replace Nielsen’s analysts. Users can escalate complex questions to the company’s research specialists, with the platform handling “fast, factual and repeatable” questions while bespoke, strategic and methodological work remains with analysts.

“The aim is not to replace that expertise; it is to free it for the work only a person should do,” says Selikane.

Future developments will add total audience sports consumption and viewership data, giving clients greater visibility of how fans follow, watch and subscribe to sports across different platforms.

For broadcasters and advertisers, this could provide a more detailed picture of where sports audiences consume content and how that behaviour is changing.

Nielsen also plans to add verified sports sponsorship news, deal announcements and other proprietary research to the platform.

Further ahead, SIYA is expected to incorporate travel and tourism data, allowing brands and rights holders to explore how sports fans travel, where they stay and what influences their travel decisions.

“Ultimately, every piece of in-house research we conduct will feed into SIYA, creating a continually growing source of verified data and insight that connects fan attitudes, behaviours, consumption and commercial activity in one place,” Selikane says.

title: Springboks handed Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu injury scare
article_text:
Springboks boss Rassie Erasmus has been handed a fresh injury scare after Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu was forced off during South Africa's 66-7 demolition of Italy.

The 24-year-old had been outstanding in Turin, earning a perfect 10/10 in RUCK's player ratings.

But his afternoon ended early after he took a blow to the jaw during an aerial contest.

His smart mouthguard reportedly triggered an alert, with the fly-half subsequently taken off for a head injury assessment (HIA).

It remains unclear whether Feinberg-Mngomezulu passed the assessment, with South Africa yet to confirm the outcome.

It was a frustrating end to an otherwise brilliant afternoon for the young playmaker.

Feinberg-Mngomezulu had been at the heart of everything good about the Springboks' attack, contributing 21 points as the world champions tore Italy apart.

His performance was good enough for a rare 10/10 from RUCK.

Now Erasmus faces an anxious wait to discover whether his first-choice fly-half will be available for the next Test.

Any return will depend on the outcome of his medical assessments and the relevant concussion protocols.

Feinberg-Mngomezulu was not the only concern to emerge from the victory.

Salmaan Moerat was withdrawn from the starting side after picking up an injury during the warm-up.

“Salmaan’s got back spasms,” Erasmus told reporters post-match in the north-west of Italy. “He had a little bit on Thursday, but we thought it would clear up and he looked good at the captain’s run.

“But unfortunately in the warm-up, he got more back spasms. So hopefully it’s not too serious.

“But ja, he’s the only casualty we had in the game. I don’t think there are any other serious injuries.”

Replacement flanker Paul de Villiers also underwent an HIA during the second half.

That leaves Erasmus with three players to assess ahead of South Africa's next international against France in Paris on Friday, 13 November.

The Springboks certainly didn't have many problems on the scoreboard.

They ran in nine tries against a helpless Italy side, with Malcolm Marx grabbing a brace in a one-sided contest.

But the fitness of Feinberg-Mngomezulu will now be a major talking point in the build-up to their next Test.

title: England A run riot against Argentina XV with emphatic 59–24 victory in Bath
article_text:
England A delivered an impressive attacking display to defeat Argentina XV 59–24 at The Recreation Ground in Bath on Friday evening, scoring nine tries in an entertaining encounter.

The result was built on an outstanding attacking performance, although Argentina showed plenty of resilience in the opening half and made England work hard for their eventual victory.

England made an explosive start, with winger Noah Caluori crossing for an early try inside the opening two minutes.

Argentina responded positively, however, with Rodrigo Fernández Criado and Pedro Delgado both finding the try line to give the visitors a 14–7 advantage.

England's response came through Max Ojomoh, whose try brought the scores level. Charlie Atkinson and Caluori then added further tries as the home side began to establish control.

Argentina continued to threaten, with Santiago Pernas crossing before the interval.

Despite the visitors' determined efforts, England went into half-time holding a 28–19 lead.

England emerged for the second half determined to put the contest beyond Argentina.

Jack Kenningham and Jamie Blamire both crossed the line to extend the home side's advantage.

Argentina refused to give up, with Federico Serpa adding another try, but England's attacking quality ultimately proved decisive.

Luke Northmore scored twice as England continued to exploit gaps in the Argentine defence, while Tobias Elliott also got on the scoresheet.

With nine tries in total, England finished the evening with a convincing 59–24 victory.

Noah Caluori was one of England's major attacking threats, finishing with two tries and demonstrating his finishing ability.

Centre Luke Northmore also enjoyed an excellent evening, crossing twice, while Max Ojomoh made an important contribution to England's attacking play.

Charlie Atkinson helped provide direction in the backs, while England's forwards contributed significantly to the team's ability to build pressure and create scoring opportunities.

The victory provided plenty of encouragement for England, particularly in the attacking department.

Scoring nine tries against Argentina XV demonstrated the potential within the squad, while the performances of younger players such as Caluori and Ojomoh will give the coaching staff plenty to consider.

There will nevertheless be defensive aspects to review. Argentina managed four tries and caused England problems during the first half, demonstrating that there is still room for improvement.

Ultimately, however, England A will take considerable confidence from a convincing 59–24 victory in Bath.

Kim Yoo-jung–Lee Yu-rim upset Chinese duo to reach Korea Open final
article_text:
Kim Yoo-jung–Lee Yu-rim pair (Samsung Life Insurance) upheld the pride of Korea's women's doubles badminton. They toppled the Chinese pair and secured a ticket to the final.

The world No. 31 Kim Yoo-jung–Lee Yu-rim pair crushed China's Chen Pan-sutian–Luo Shu-min pair (world No. 66) 2-0 (21-17, 21-11) in the semifinals of the 2026 Badminton World Federation (BWF) World Tour Korea Open (Super 500) women's doubles at Jinnam Gymnasium in Yeosu on the 7th and advanced to the final.

Although Chen Pan-sutian–Luo Shu-min have low world rankings, they are a strong duo that won two Super 500 events this year. After first teaming up in May, they won the Malaysia Masters and later topped the Arctic Open in October. In particular, Luo Shu-min paired with Li Jing to win the Asian Championships women's doubles gold this year, showing her caliber.

The Chinese pair seized the early momentum. Kim Yoo-jung–Lee Yu-rim fell behind 2-6 after a series of defensive errors. But the Korean pair calmly chipped away point by point and came back to lead 8-7. Kim Yoo-jung then added points with powerful attacks, and they reached the interval leading 11-8.

Korea's momentum continued after the break. Chen Pan-sutian–Luo Shu-min's counterattack was not easy to handle, but with steady defense the Koreans maintained a 3–4 point gap. Kim Yoo-jung–Lee Yu-rim conceded consecutive points late in the game and were chased to 19-17, but they added two points in a row to reach 21 first.

The second game was tight as well. Both teams played a seesaw game, trading leads. But Kim Yoo-jung and Lee Yu-rim showed excellent concentration at 6-6, forced the opponents into errors and scored four consecutive points to pull ahead.

Their finishing power was even greater. Kim Yoo-jung–Lee Yu-rim went on a five-point run led by Lee Yu-rim's attacks from 15-11. In an instant they reached match point at 20-11. The opponents' return then hit the net, confirming their first Super 500 final appearance.

With this, Kim Yoo-jung–Lee Yu-rim reached the final at their home tournament and upheld the pride of Korea's women's doubles. The previous day, Kim Hye-jung–Lee Yeon-woo pair was eliminated in the round of 16 after losing to Japan's Hirokami Rui–Hobara Sayaka pair.

Since forming a new doubles team this year, Kim Yoo-jung and Lee Yu-rim have shown a steep rise. They reached the quarterfinals of the Indonesia Masters (Super 500) in January, won the Indonesia International Challenge in August, and in September captured the Vietnam Open (Super 100), marking their first World Tour title.

They added the achievement of reaching their first Super 500 semifinal in this tournament. After the round of 16 win, Kim Yoo-jung said she really did not expect to win and could not imagine it, and that it really did not feel real. She said it came to her later: "Ah, I really won." Lee Yu-rim promised, "In tomorrow's semifinal I will play confidently and do everything I want to do."

As promised, Kim Yoo-jung–Lee Yu-rim defeated the Chinese pair and advanced to the final. Their final opponent will be the winner of the match between the American Lauren Lam–Allison Quinn Lee pair (world No. 15) and the Japanese Hirokami Rui–Hobara Sayaka pair (world No. 17).

'Respect the guys who stayed loyal' - Dan Bradbury on LIV backtrackers, DP World Tour play-offs and his PGA Tour ambitions
article_text:
Dan Bradbury hopes the DP World Tour will honour those players that stayed loyal to it amid the flood of golfers backtracking from LIV, as he himself plots his own route away from the circuit where he has made his name the last four years.

But where a huge swathe of golfers were guilty of deserting the DP World Tour four years ago and are now queueing up to return with their tails between their legs, the only exit route Bradbury wants to take is via a promotion.

For the 27-year-old from Wakefield went into the final two weeks of the season in the Middle East firmly in the hunt for one of the 10 tickets to the PGA Tour available to the leading players on the Race to Dubai rankings not already exempt.

Whether he earns one or not via a strong performance in Abu Dhabi this week or Dubai next, Bradbury is content with his lot.

The thought of playing in America where he went to university for five years, excites him a lot. But if not, the DP World Tour - with bigger names coming back - is a not-too distant second best.

“For all I talk about coming to play well, it is pretty much the only thing that’s left on the table for me now,” said Bradbury, who came into this week 19th on the rankings, with 14th spot currently the target to snag a ticket to the PGA Tour.

“I’ve already qualified for Dubai which is great, some lads are here this week playing to get into next week, so I‘ve not got that pressure.

“PGA Tour is only a bonus. We’re still very lucky playing on the DP World Tour and we play a great schedule, we play great events.

“But the PGA Tour is where you want to be.

“I’ve got nothing to lose at this point. The DP World Tour is still great and if I get a PGA Tour card it would be amazing for my career, but there’s no pressure on it.”

LIV Golf’s emergence in the summer of 2022 shook the sport to its foundations, sparking constant evolution by the existing tours to keep up and retain their star players.

One of the changes was the PGA Tour offering cards to the top 10 on the DP World Tour, something Bradbury’s fellow Yorkshiremen John Parry and Dan Brown took advantage of last season.

This could be the last season for it to be as cut and dried as that, with the PGA Tour moving to a two-tier circuit in 2028 with an elite Championship Series and secondary Challenger Series – with the route to it from Europe’s premier circuit yet to be decided.

It means this year might be Bradbury’s best chance to take the leap onto the PGA Tour as everyone knows it.

“This year is probably…not the last chance, but it feels like it’s a lot more significant than it might be next year,” admitted Bradbury.

“Fortunately DP World Tour is in a good place at the minute with everyone wanting to come back here to play, so who knows. I think the DP World Tour will be in a stronger place in a year’s time as well.”

Fields for the 2027 DP World Tour season are set to be swelled by players who have jumped LIV’s sinking ship, most notably European Ryder Cup stars Jon Rahm, Tyrell Hatton and Sergio Garcia.

Their return has not gone down well with some players who chose to stay loyal to the DP World Tour, with Eddie Pepperell one of the most outspoken critics of the returning players.

For his part, Bradbury sees it from both sides.

“As long as the tour shows respect to the guys who showed them their loyalty,” he told The Yorkshire Post this week.

“They should be the priority, the guys that didn’t go.

“But there’s so many grey areas. If I say to you this person wants an invite, would they add to this field? You and I might have different opinions on that.

"So it’s going to be very difficult for the tour to get it right and to draw the line in the right place.

“But I think overall we will have better fields next year and we will benefit from it.

“The tour itself will be in a better place but there’s going to be some very disgruntled members that lose out if there’s only 100 cards and we suddenly let loads back.

“It’s going to be a hard one to judge and it’s hard to say right now what the right thing to do is.

“Overall the tour will be in a better place with some household names back, as long as they respect the guys that did have the chance to go but chose not to. Look after your members first, but if you can help your members by making better events, then fine.”

Whether he wins or finishes down the field in Abu Dhabi and Dubai the next two weeks, Bradbury is in line for his best ever finish on the DP World Tour.

Two years ago he came home 30th, but last year he didn’t even qualify for the end-of-season play-offs.

“I missed them last year so it’s nice to be back, that’s for sure,” said Bradbury, whose victory at the Joburg Open in March was the season highlight.

title: Miyazaki suffers comeback loss, exits Korea Open before Ahn Se-young showdown
article_text:
"Japan's badminton idol" Miyazaki Tomoka (20) was eliminated before she could meet Ahn Se-young (24, Samsung Life Insurance), who had said she wanted to try again. She packed her bags after suffering a come-from-behind loss to an opponent she had beaten seven times in their meetings.

World No. 7 Miyazaki lost in the women's singles quarterfinals of the 2026 Badminton World Federation (BWF) World Tour Korea Open (Super 500) held June 6 at Jinnam Gymnasium in Yeosu, Jeonnam, to fellow Japanese Akechi Hina (world No. 16), 1-2 (21-13, 21-23, 8-21).

It was an unexpected result. Before the match Miyazaki had a 7-0 record against Akechi. She was also nine spots higher in the world rankings. Miyazaki was expected to have the edge this time as well, but the result was the opposite.

The start was good. Miyazaki pressed Akechi from the first game and won 21-13. Miyazaki, who had an overwhelming advantage in their head-to-head record, seemed on course to reach the semifinals easily.

But the momentum changed from the second game. Akechi fought stubbornly and the match went to deuce. Miyazaki did not give up easily, but she gradually fell behind in the physical battle and lost 21-23. In the final third game, exhausted, Miyazaki managed only eight points and was defeated.

With that, Miyazaki's potential semifinal showdown with Ahn Se-young was canceled. He had not hidden his desire to test himself against Ahn Se-young after winning his round of 16 match the day before.

At the time Miyazaki said in a broadcast interview, "I would like to face Ahn Se-young if possible, but I cannot guarantee victory (in the next match) yet," adding, "Still, because the possibility is not completely out of the question, I want to do my best to challenge it."

He also said, "There are parts where my preparation is insufficient, but when I face Ahn Se-young I want to see how far I can go. I want to play while showing my game as well as possible, and above all I want to steady my mindset and take on the challenge," adding, "I want to emulate Ahn Se-young's physical aspects."

In fact, Miyazaki had met Ahn Se-young eight times and had never beaten her. Their most recent meeting was the final of the China Masters last September, where she was swept 0-2. Although she has emerged as the next-generation leader of Japanese badminton, she has yet to get past the Ahn Se-young barrier.

Despite saying she wanted to challenge Ahn Se-young again, Miyazaki lost to Akechi, who had previously beaten her seven times, and did not even get that opportunity. Showing clear signs of fatigue on court, Miyazaki left the venue quickly after the match, declining mixed-zone interviews.

By contrast, Ahn Se-young is cruising toward her 11th title of the season. World No. 1 Ahn Se-young demolished Japan's KUNJI Riko (world No. 20) 2-0 (21-7, 21-13) in the quarterfinals held the same day. The match lasted only 37 minutes.

Ahn Se-young extended her winning streak to 53 matches. Her international record this season stands at 70 matches with 69 wins and one loss, a winning percentage of 98.57%. She has not lost since the All England Open final in March, where she fell to Wang Zhiyi (China).

Ahn Se-young's semifinal opponent will be Akechi instead of Miyazaki. After facing Kunji, she will again face another Japanese player. If she wins here, she could meet her "rival" Yamaguchi Akane (world No. 2) in the final.<

title: Patrick Pellegrini the difference-maker as Tonga survive Romania scare
article_text:
Tonga improved to 2-2 in the Nations Cup with a dramatic 43-38 win over Romania in Bucharest, largely thanks to the creativity of playmaker Patrick Pellegrini.

The execution of the No.10’s audacious tactical kicking inspired three of Tonga’s six tries, and his goal-kicking made the difference in a match where Romania also dotted down six times.

Romania enjoyed a hot start in attack, breaking the line in the second minute before a desperate defence rejected them. They were back in the Tongan 22 moments later when a chip kick was collected, and Marius Simionescu proceeded to slip through a gap and reach the line.

Tonga were yet to get an opportunity to attack when Romania spilled the ball on halfway in the seventh minute, leading to a storming Siegfried Fisiihoi break from broken play. The prop was dragged down five metres from the line, but a well-placed crossfield kick from Pellegrini found an overlap on the wing, which Veikoso Poloniati exploited for Tonga’s opening score.

Romania’s first scrum suggested the Europeans had the upper hand, but the contest evened out from there. The hosts’ first lineout of the night was picked off, but Tonga were then unable to disrupt Tudor Butnariu’s precise throwing until much later in the Test.

By the 16th minute, Tonga had their second try via a superb piece of agility from fullback Taniela Filimone, who broke the line and had the pace to swerve around the final defender and score.

There were a handful of powerful hits from the Tongan defence in the opening quarter, and a John Tapueluelu hit in the 18th minute saw the ball hit the deck, with the winger then diving on the scraps. Another masterful kick from Pellegrini sat up perfectly for Anzelo Tuitavuki, and suddenly play was back inside Romania’s 22. Clever passing ensured the visitors exploited another overlap when the ball swung back to Tapueluelu’s wing, and he finished the play he had started a minute earlier.

The score was 19-7 in favour of the Tongans by the 20th minute, but Romania started to reverse the momentum with some more of the attacking form they showed in the opening minutes. In the 25th minute, it was a rolling maul that got Iulian Hartig over the line.

Tonga got over the line from a rolling maul of their own shortly after play resumed, but the play was called back for obstruction. Romania had found their recipe for success and went straight back to it with their next opportunity, scoring again with a try by Butnariu.

Pellegrini would have the final say of the half, though, with a penalty extending Tonga’s lead to 22-17 at the break.

Poloniati had the first big play of the second half, stealing an exposed ball behind Romania’s first ruck from the kick-off. Lotu Inisi provided the power to get his side on the front foot, and once again it was Pellegrini’s boot that set up a try for Tuitavuki.

Romania were denied another rolling maul try by an illegal Tongan defensive act, but wouldn’t be stopped with their next crack at the line. The theme of Tonga responding swiftly continued when debutant Efi Maafu took the field in the 54th minute and scored immediately, crashing over at the back of a Tongan rolling maul.

Trailing by 12 with 16 minutes remaining, Romania had a lineout inside Tonga’s 22 stolen, but executed after Tonga’s clearance and quickly powered their way into scoring range before Gheorghe Gajion scored an opportunistic try right under the posts.

Tonga’s lead was down to five when they conceded successive set-piece penalties and Romania’s attack roared to life, with Taylor Gontineac winning back a contestable kick. Play got frantic when Tonga were penalised for a high tackle, but Simionescu missed touch with his kick. Filimone claimed a contestable kick seconds later and ignited a break, only for Romania to make a breakdown steal and immediately knock the ball on at the base of the ruck.

Tonga’s final points of the night came from Toma Taufa in the 70th minute, leaving Romania 10 minutes to score twice. Six minutes of tough Tongan defence later, the hosts were held up over the line. With 35 seconds remaining on the clock, Gajion powered over for his second try.

A quick and successful conversion from Gabriel Rupanu ensured there was time for a restart, but the halfback then sealed his team’s fate with a knock-on at the base of a ruck 45 seconds later. Tonga emerged as 43-38 victors.

title: "Roots run deep" – All Blacks legend Richie McCaw was asked to play for Scotland
article_text:
Richie McCaw is one of the greatest players in rugby history, but the former All Blacks captain has a surprising connection to Scotland.

The two-time Rugby World Cup winner has Scottish ancestry on both sides of his family. He was even jokingly asked to swap the famous black jersey for Scotland's blue.

And there is plenty more to the 148-cap legend than his extraordinary rugby career.

From his dramatic body transformation to his sporting wife, three children and unlikely second career as a helicopter pilot, McCaw has lived a fascinating life.

Here are 10 things you might not know about the New Zealand icon.

1. He was asked to swap New Zealand for Scotland

McCaw's Scottish roots run deep, with both sides of his family tracing their ancestry back to the country.

In 2014, researchers at Glasgow's Mitchell Library discovered that his great-great-great-grandfather, Alexander McCaw, was born in Girvan, Ayrshire, in 1808.

The findings prompted a cheeky suggestion from VisitScotland chairman Mike Cantlay, who asked whether McCaw would consider pulling on Scotland's famous blue jersey.

McCaw himself had spoken warmly about his Scottish connections, admitting he always loved visiting the country.

There was never a serious international switch on the cards, but the discovery certainly raised a few smiles.

McCaw has undergone a remarkable physical transformation since hanging up his boots.

During his playing days, the powerful flanker weighed around 107–110kg.

However, his move into endurance racing saw his weight drop considerably.

His incredible 27kg body transformation has previously attracted plenty of attention, with the former captain swapping rugby training for endurance challenges.

McCaw married former New Zealand hockey international Gemma Flynn in January 2017.

Gemma represented the Black Sticks at the Olympic Games and enjoyed a successful international career.

The couple share a passion for sport and have even competed in endurance events together.

Away from rugby, McCaw is a devoted family man.

He and Gemma have three daughters, with their youngest arriving in April 2023.

The former captain has spoken about how becoming a father brought a completely different set of challenges compared with leading the All Blacks.

While many rugby legends head into coaching or punditry, McCaw chose a very different path.

The former All Blacks captain became a commercial helicopter pilot.

His love of aviation began as a child, with his grandfather introducing him to gliding.

McCaw later helped deliver supplies and rescue people following the devastating Kaikōura earthquake in 2016.

6. He played the bagpipes with The Wiggles

Perhaps one of McCaw's most unexpected appearances came in 2021.

The famously tough former flanker joined children's entertainment group The Wiggles on stage in Christchurch.

Wearing a special black Wiggles jersey, McCaw played the bagpipes during a performance of Scotland the Brave.

He even joined the group's famous Fruit Salad singalong.

7. He completed a brutal 666km adventure race

McCaw's competitive streak didn't disappear when he retired.

He has competed in GODZone, one of New Zealand's toughest adventure races.

The gruelling event involves mountain biking, kayaking, trekking and navigating remote terrain.

One challenge covered approximately 666km and took his team around six days to complete.

8. He played through a broken foot to win the World Cup

McCaw's toughness was legendary throughout his career.

During the 2011 Rugby World Cup, he played through a stress fracture in his foot.

Despite the pain, the All Blacks captain helped lead New Zealand to a dramatic 8-7 victory over France in the final.

Four years later, he lifted the Webb Ellis Cup again after beating Australia 34-17 at Twickenham.

9. He wrote his rugby ambitions on a McDonald's napkin

Long before becoming an All Blacks legend, McCaw set himself some extraordinary goals.

During a visit to McDonald's with his uncle, he wrote down his ambitions on a napkin.

McCaw eventually made his international debut against Ireland in 2001, aged just 20.

He went on to win 148 caps, recording an incredible 131 victories.

10. He received New Zealand's highest honour

McCaw was appointed to the Order of New Zealand following his retirement in 2015.

It is the country's highest honour, with membership limited to 20 living people at any one time.

He also won World Rugby Player of the Year three times and was inducted into the World Rugby Hall of Fame in 2019.

Despite his extraordinary achievements, McCaw has largely avoided the spotlight since retirement, preferring family life, flying and adventure racing.
